title: Humiliation for Obama! Congress crushes his veto and the Saudi 9/11 bill becomes law
text: It was a stunning rebuke. Congress on Wednesday overwhelmingly smashed President Barack Obama's veto of legislation allowing relatives of the victims of the Sept. 11 attacks to sue Saudi Arabia. The first veto override of his entire presidency, and it came just four months before that presidency ends. The House of Representatives voted a crushing 348-77 against the veto, hours after the Senate threw it out 97-1. The result? The “Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act” will become law. The vote was a brutal blow to Obama, and to Saudi Arabia, one of the United States' longest-standing allies in the Arab world. And some lawmakers who backed the override already plan to revisit the issue. Obama hit back, saying he thought the Congress had made a mistake. He repeated his warning that the legislation set a dangerous precedent and suggested politics was behind the vote. “If you're perceived as voting against 9/11 families right before an election, not surprisingly, that's a hard vote for people to take. But it would have been the right thing to do,” he said on CNN. His 11 previous vetoes were all sustained. Not this time. Almost all of his strongest Democratic supporters in Congress abandoned him and joined Republicans, in one of their last acts before leaving Washington to campaign for the Nov. 8 election. “Overriding a presidential veto is something we don't take lightly, but it was important in this case that the families of the victims of 9/11 be allowed to pursue justice, even if that pursuit causes some diplomatic discomforts,” Senator Charles Schumer, a top Senate Democrat, said in a statement. Schumer represents New York, site of the World Trade Center and home to many of the nearly 3,000 people killed in the 2001 attacks, survivors and families of victims. Who could vote against them?

title: Retired four-star general criticises Trump over NFL anthem comments: ‘Put Me Down With Kaepernick’
text: Donald Trump's criticism of black athletes who sit rather than stand during the national anthem in protest of racial inequality and police brutality has drawn a backlash. Gen. Michael Hayden, a retired United States Air Force four-star general who served in the military for 39 years, wrote a column strongly criticising the former reality television star over his posts on Twitter about the NFL. Hayden was initially not enthusiastic about supporting Colin Kaepernick, the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback who started the silent protest of kneeling during the anthem. Hayden, who served as national security adviser and head of the CIA after he left the military, wrote that the issues Kaepernick raised were both real and sincerely held. His position changed when Trump spoke to a crowd in strongly Republican Alabama and called black athletes who kneel sons of bitches. Hayden wrote that this was consistent with how Trump has previously treated other groups, such as Mexicans (murderers and rapists), intelligence professionals (Nazis), immigrants (deeply unfair), refugees (dangerous) and Muslims (they hate us). As a 39-year military veteran, I think I know something about the flag, the anthem, patriotism, and I think I know why we fight, he wrote. It's not to allow the president to divide us by wrapping himself in the national banner. I never imagined myself saying this before Friday, but if now forced to choose in this dispute, put me down with Kaepernick. Trump criticises everyone, particularly minorities, in order to mobilise his base. He favours conflict and chaos. Electing a former reality television star to lead the most powerful country on earth invites controversy, and that is what Trump's base wants.

title: Florida gun-rights advocate shot in the back by her 4-year-old son while driving
text: Jamie Gilt is a resident of Florida. She is a Ted Cruz supporter and a pro-gun advocate who runs a pro-gun Facebook page called Jamie Gilt for Gun Sense, which appears to have been named to mock firearm safety groups. According to the pages she has liked on Facebook, she admires the Tea Party, is a horse enthusiast, believes Hillary Clinton belongs in prison and admires the terrorist group that engaged in an armed standoff with the federal government at Bundy Ranch. She is also the kind of person who would leave a loaded gun within reach of a 4-year-old. On Tuesday afternoon, a Putnam County Sheriff's Deputy noticed a woman behaving frantically inside her four-door pickup truck. The officer soon realised that the woman inside the vehicle had been shot, according to Captain Joseph Wells. The woman told the officer that she had been shot by her four-year-old son, who was sitting in the back seat, while the two were travelling to her sister's home to pick up a horse. She was shot through the seat and the round went through her back, Wells said. He noted that there were no holes in the back of the truck, which had a horse trailer hitched to it. The child was not strapped into his booster seat when the deputy found Gilt. There was a booster seat in the back of the vehicle, but however the boy was not strapped in when the deputy got to them, Wells said.

title: Paul Ryan makes a request of Donald Trump that the Trump campaign will not welcome
text: House Speaker Paul Ryan compromised his principles when he endorsed Donald Trump for president of the United States. He did so without conviction, and timed the endorsement to coincide with a major policy speech by Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton, which drew attention away from it. Since then, the relationship between Ryan and Trump has been cool, and the two have never appeared on stage together. During a weekly press briefing, Ryan was asked a question that many have raised: why has Donald Trump not released his tax returns? The question has become more pressing because Newsweek has published a critical report showing that, should Donald Trump become president, the Trump Organization's questionable network of international ties would endanger the national security of the United States of America. Following that report, it is more important than before that the American electorate sees Trump's tax returns. Even George W. Bush's ethics lawyer said that these ties are a, quote, serious problem. Ryan then said that Trump's returns need to be made public. He first referred to his own release of his tax returns when he ran for Vice President: I did release my returns. I'll defer to Donald Trump as to when he thinks the appropriate time to release his returns. I know he is under audit, and he has an opinion on when to release those and I'll defer to him on that. He then qualified his position, out of concern about upsetting Trump's supporters, and said: I released mine. I think he should release his. I'll leave it to him when to do it. Ryan needs to take a more forceful position on the issue.

title: Burgers, salads and a broken heart: the cafe owner who will never let Diana be forgotten
text: His hands were shaking. Abdul Daoud spilt most of the cappuccino into the saucer the first time he served Princess Diana, his nerves completely getting the better of him. Almost 20 years after she was killed when her car crashed in a Paris tunnel, he still works surrounded by pictures of the woman he calls the princess of the people, in a cafe he named Diana. It is his deeply personal crusade to keep her memory alive. My promise to her is to put this place as a tribute for her, he said of the cafe, set up in 1989 near London's Kensington Gardens, home to the palace where Diana used to live. For him, celebrating her life is simply business as usual. Here visitors can eat Diana salads or Diana burgers, and here, he said, she used to stop by regularly. Imagine that! She is the princess of the people, always, he said, insisting he does not believe she will ever be forgotten. But will she? Many younger Britons said that while they understand the fascination with the princess, whose painful struggles to fit in to the royal household played out in the full, merciless glare of the media, they simply don't feel it themselves. I think she maybe meant more to my mother, said Stephen Butler in the west London area where Diana used to live. When she died I remember my mother shaking me awake and being quite devastated about it. Student Shermine Grigorius was just three years old when Diana died, but after hearing stories about the Princess of Wales from her mother, she sees her as a symbol of kindness. The royals have always been dutifully charitable. Diana was something else: she was known for going far beyond her in-laws, or even any celebrity of the time, in her philanthropy.

title: Fake tweet appears to show FBI support for Donald Trump
text: Composer and frequent Twitter user Nick Harvey shared a tweet that he said he had noticed from the FBI, which appeared to announce the agency's strong support for Donald Trump. The tweet was not genuine. It is the latest humorous fake tweet produced by Harvey. Earlier examples include one presented as coming from Vine, which read: Nicely done, Vine. Nicely done. Another was a reply to Steven Woolfe presented as coming from UKIP, captioned: UKIP there, being as classy as ever. A third was presented as coming from the official Mrs Brown's Boys account, captioned: Twitter at its best. Harvey also claimed to have written one genuine but controversial tweet from a celebrity. His tweets have deceived many users, leading one to comment “someone needs to take that fake tweet creator app away from you asap”. The publication does not share that view.

title: 70 years of men at the top! Women senators demand Obama fight for first female U.N. chief
text: Seventy years. That is how long men have held the top job at the United Nations. Now seven U.S. women senators are pushing back hard. On Thursday they urged President Barack Obama to fight for the election of the world body's first female secretary-general later this year. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, a former South Korean foreign minister, is due to step down at the end of 2016 after two five-year terms. A man has held the post since the organization's inception 70 years ago. Isn't it time for change? The powerful 15-member Security Council, including veto powers China, Russia, the United States, Britain and France, will recommend a candidate for election by the 193-member General Assembly to succeed Ban. “We ask that the United States play a leading role in pressing for the strong consideration of qualified women,” the seven Democratic senators wrote to Obama. Led by Barbara Boxer, a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the letter was also signed by senators Patty Murray, Mazie Hirono, Tammy Baldwin, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeanne Shaheen and Barbara Mikulski. The administration's answer? Cautious. A senior Obama administration official said: “While we would welcome the selection of a woman as the next Secretary-General, we will ultimately support the best candidate of either gender.” Meanwhile the pressure is mounting: Fifty-three 53 countries, led by Colombia, are pushing for a female secretary-general, and several civil society groups are lobbying for a woman to lead the organization. Seven candidates have been put forward, three of them women: U.N. cultural organization (UNESCO) Director-General Irina Bokova, former Croatian Foreign Minister Vesna Pusic and Moldova's former Foreign Minister Natalia Gherman. The other four are former Macedonian Foreign Minister Srgjan Kerim, Montenegro Foreign Minister Igor Luksic, former Slovenian President Danilo Turk and former U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Antonio Guterres.

title: WikiLeaks emails show Clinton campaign coordination with Soros foundation on police reform and implicit bias
text: Emails from the personal email account of Hillary Clinton campaign manager John Podesta, published by WikiLeaks, show that the Clinton campaign coordinated with George Soros's Open Society Foundations on police reform. Soros, who has given almost $10 million to the Clinton super PAC Priorities USA, is a major funder of Black Lives Matter. The Washington Times reported in August that Soros has given at least $33 million to the group through the Open Society Foundations (OSF), which he funds and controls. Both OSF and Clinton have called for action against implicit bias among police officers. A December 2015 email exchange between Podesta and OSF president Chris Stone was included in the batch of Podesta's emails released by WikiLeaks on Friday. Hi, John. Your policy team was asking me for ideas on police reform a couple of months ago. Here's a concrete idea I've written up, and a good hook for it in Chicago, Stone wrote. Stone attached to the email an article he had written that advocated putting federally funded bureaucrats in charge of police oversight.

title: Top U.S. nuclear commander: I'm assuming North Korea set off a hydrogen bomb!
text: It is the assumption everyone feared. The U.S. general in charge of America's nuclear forces said on Thursday he was working on the basis that North Korea really did test a hydrogen bomb on Sept. 3, crossing a chilling threshold in its weapons development. Pyongyang immediately boasted that it had successfully tested a hydrogen bomb. Until now, the United States had declined to say what it was. Not anymore. Air Force General John Hyten, head of the U.S. military's Strategic Command, said he had a responsibility, as the military officer responsible for responding to the test, to assume it was a hydrogen bomb, based on the sheer size of the blast. I'm assuming it was a hydrogen bomb. I have to make that assumption as a military officer, Hyten told a small group of reporters who were accompanying Defense Secretary Jim Mattie on a trip to Hyten's headquarters in Nebraska. I'm not a nuclear scientist, so I can't tell you this is how it worked, this is what the bomb was. ... But I can tell you the size that we observed and saw tends to me to indicate that it was a hydrogen bomb and I have to figure out what the right response is with our allies as to that kind of event. And how big was it? The North Korean nuclear test was its sixth and by far its most powerful, and it pushed the U.N. Security Council to step up sanctions. It came after a string of North Korean missile tests, including one that flew over Japan and another that the U.S. judged to be an inter-continental ballistic missile (ICBM). And the provocations keep coming: South Korea's military said shortly after Hyten's remarks that North Korea had fired an unidentified missile eastward from the Sunan district in its capital, Pyongyang.

title: Brazil's elite preach austerity – while handing themselves fat raises!
text: Brazil's sickly economy is bleeding thousands of jobs a day. States are scrambling to pay police officers and teachers. Money for subsidized meals is so scarce that one legislator suggested the poor could “eat every other day. ” Shocking? Wait. Not everyone is suffering. Civil servants in the judicial branch are enjoying a 41 percent raise. Legislators in São Paulo, Brazil's largest city, voted to boost their own salaries by more than 26 percent. And Congress, which is getting ready to cut pension benefits across the country, now lets its own members retire with lifelong pensions after just two years in office. Two years! title: The year our clothes went to war: how politics hijacked fashion
text: Politics invaded our closets this year. Clothes stopped being mere products and became battle lines. It began in early February, when Beyoncé stormed onto the field at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., for the Super Bowl 50 halftime show, followed by an army of backup dancers in outfits paying homage to the Black Panthers, to perform “Formation,” a song hailed as the anthem of the Black Lives Matter movement. From that moment it was obvious that “fashion statement” was going to take on a whole new meaning in 2016. Telling people what you believed was no longer enough. You had to show them. And the simplest, most powerful, most public way to do that? What you wore. In a world of white noise and factional cacophony, a world where the first line of communication is visual, clothes are our shared language. Love it or hate it, you can read it. Once upon a time “political dress” meant the dress of the political class. In 2016, everyone donned it, and some damned it. Practically every month brought a new clash. In April, Laurence Rossignol, the French minister for women's rights, fired the opening shot at what became the fashion lightning rod of the summer: the Burkini. Ms. Rossignol lashed out at designers from Marks Spencer to Dolce Gabbana for catering to the Muslim market with swimsuits and hijabs, accusing them of “promoting women's bodies being locked up” to fatten their own coffers. Soon Pierre Bergé, the outspoken of Yves Saint Laurent, charged into the fray. One item of clothing had become a symbol of the fight over the balance between enlightenment values and civil society, and over whether freedom includes the freedom to wear whatever you want.

title: Why John McCain will not vote to repeal and replace Obamacare

A vote would set the stage for another major decision in Congress on the 2010 law, which brought health insurance to millions of Americans and became former Democratic President Barack Obama's signature domestic achievement.

title: “Particularly ugly”: rights group sounds alarm over Trump refugee ban and return of torture sites
text: A stark warning. Human Rights Watch (HRW) said on Wednesday that U.S. President Donald Trump is “closing the door” on people fleeing Islamic State and may try to reopen secret detention centers where torture can be used. It called on Congress to step in. A temporary ban on refugees that Trump is expected to sign this week is a “particularly ugly” policy among a raft of populist initiatives that could also breach the U.S. Constitution, the rights group said. Trump looks set to “stop refugee admissions to the United States, ostensibly on security grounds,” HRW head Kenneth Roth told a news briefing in Geneva. “But in order to score a political point at home, Trump is closing the door on them. That is one particularly ugly aspect of what he is doing.” And he went further. “It's as if Trump is indifferent to the extraordinary suffering that many of these refugees have been through. Many of these people are fleeing ISIS (Islamic State), or the ISIS equivalents around the world,” he said. HRW, one of the biggest international human rights groups, based in the United States, said it feared Trump would “start refilling Guantanamo” and might use “dark sites” on foreign soil for detainees. Secret prisons, again? “One thing we expect either today or later this week is an order from Trump to begin exploring ... the resumption of CIA dark sites,” said Roth, an American. On Wednesday The Washington Post published a draft executive order, “Detention and Interrogation of Enemy Combatants”, that could open the way for terrorism suspects to be interrogated in secret prisons abroad. “Last time, these black sites were often in democracies - they were in Poland, Latvia, Romania, if you look around the world, they were in places like Morocco, Egypt, Jordan, Thailand, Afghanistan,” Roth said.

title: Caught flat-footed! U.S. had no plan as Russia's disinformation blitz hit the election
text: More than a decade of preparation, and still blindsided. The U.S. government spent years getting ready to respond to malicious hacking by a foreign power, yet had no clear strategy when Russia unleashed a disinformation campaign over the internet during the U.S. election campaign, current and former White House cyber security advisers said. Where did all the effort go? Far more went into plotting offensive hacking and preparing defenses against the less likely but more dramatic damage from electronic assaults on the power grid, the financial system or direct manipulation of voting machines. Over the last several years, U.S. intelligence agencies watched Russia use coordinated hacking and disinformation in Ukraine and elsewhere, the advisers and intelligence experts said. But there was little sustained, high-level government conversation about the risk of that propaganda reaching the United States. Then, during the presidential election, it did, to an extent that may have changed the outcome, the security sources said. And U.S. officials felt their hands were tied in investigating Russian-supported propaganda because of free speech guarantees in the Constitution. A former White House official warned that any U.S. government attempt to counter the flow of foreign state-backed disinformation through deterrence would run into major political, legal and moral obstacles. “You would have to have massive surveillance and curtailed freedom and that is a cost we have not been willing to accept,” said the former official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “They (Russia) can control distribution of information in ways we don't.” A troubling admission. Clinton Watts, a security consultant, former FBI agent and a fellow at the nonprofit Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the U.S. government no longer even has an organization, like the U.S. Information Agency, that provided counter-narratives during the Cold War.

title: Border mayor rages: Trump's wall is “offensive” and will scare off tourists!
text: The mayor of Laredo, Texas, Pete Saenz, is now branding President Donald Trump's Executive Order to begin construction of a border wall “offensive”. Offensive! And the CBS News piece? It goes out of its way to portray border walls as not necessarily working at keeping illegal immigrants out of the country and stopping the flow of drugs, even titling the piece “Critics on why building a Mexico border wall won't be effective.” Not everyone agrees. That barrier with proper manpower, resources, technology and other tools will be effective. But most important, for the first time we have a president that wants to secure the border.”

title: State Department's human trafficking report inflated ratings of 14 countries; question raised over Obama administration agenda
text: President Barack Obama has described the fight against human trafficking as one of the great human rights causes of our time and has pledged that the United States will continue to lead it. If Obama regarded human trafficking as such an important cause, it is unclear why his State Department would work to conceal information about serious human rights violators. In the weeks before a major annual U.S. report on human trafficking that publicly identifies the world's worst offenders, human rights experts at the State Department concluded that trafficking conditions had not improved in Malaysia and Cuba, and that in China conditions had worsened. The State Department's senior political staff disagreed, and their view prevailed. An examination based on interviews with more than a dozen sources in Washington and foreign capitals shows that the government office set up to independently grade global efforts to fight human trafficking was repeatedly overruled by senior American diplomats and pressured into inflating assessments of 14 strategically important countries in this year's Trafficking in Persons report. In total, analysts in the Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons, known within the U.S. government as J/TIP, disagreed with U.S. diplomatic bureaus on ratings for 17 countries, the sources said. The analysts, who specialise in assessing efforts to combat modern slavery such as the illegal trade in humans for forced labor or prostitution, won only three of those disputes, the worst ratio in the 15-year history of the unit, according to the sources. As a result, Malaysia, Cuba and China, as well as countries such as India, Uzbekistan and Mexico, received better grades than the State Department's human rights experts had recommended, the sources said.

title: Pope Francis' powerful warning: the cross is NOT jewelry!
text: A blunt message from the Pope. The Christian cross is “not an adornment for the house or a piece of jewelry to wear,” but a reminder of Christ's love in saving mankind from evil and sin, Pope Francis declared on Sunday. In his weekly Angelus message, the Pope reflected on the Sunday gospel reading that shows Jesus transfigured before three of his disciples on Mount Tabor. Christ “wanted to reveal his glory to his disciples not to prevent them from experiencing the cross, but to show where the cross leads,” Francis said. “Whoever dies with Christ, will rise again with Christ. And the cross is the door of the resurrection.” Stirring words. “Those who fight together with Him, will triumph with Him. This is the message of hope that the cross of Jesus contains, urging us to courage in our lives,” he said. Then came the warning. “The Christian cross is not a decoration for the house or a piece of jewelry to wear,” Francis continued, but “a reminder of the love with which Jesus sacrificed himself to save mankind from evil and sin.” How many of us need to hear that? Sunday's Angelus was the Pope's first public appearance since returning to Rome from a retreat in the Italian town of Ariccia. “In this Lenten season, let us devoutly contemplate the image of the crucifix, Jesus on the cross,” Francis urged on Sunday. “This is the symbol of the Christian faith, the emblem of Jesus, who died and rose for us.” “Let us make sure that the Cross marks the stages of our Lenten journey to understand ever more fully the seriousness of sin and the value of the sacrifice with which the Redeemer saved us all,” he said.
